The World Magnetic Model, produced jointly by the United States National Centers for Environmental Information and the British Geological Survey, is reissued every five years, and an unscheduled correction had to be published in early 2019 because the field had drifted outside specification ahead of schedule. The practical consequence is arithmetic. An angular error of one degree displaces you about seventeen and a half metres for every kilometre travelled. Using a thirty year old declination figure that is five degrees stale, over a four kilometre leg in poor visibility, puts you roughly three hundred and fifty metres off your intended point, which in mountains is easily the wrong valley.

sections.heading: National Series Around the World
sections.body: Britain's Ordnance Survey remains the reference point for many English speaking users. Its two walking series are the Landranger at one to fifty thousand, two hundred and four sheets in pink covers, and the Explorer at one to twenty five thousand, over four hundred sheets in orange covers showing field boundaries and rights of way. Behind them lies a continuously maintained digital database from which the paper products are drawn. The United States Geological Survey's seven and a half minute quadrangles at one to twenty four thousand are the most detailed general coverage the country has ever had, completed in 1992 after roughly fifty years of work. Since 2009 the agency has published US Topo, a digital replacement generated automatically from national databases on a rolling cycle of a few years. The trade is honest but real: US Topo is current where its source data are current, and it lacks a great deal of the field checked trail and structure detail that surveyors put onto the classic sheets. Fortunately every legacy edition has been scanned into a freely downloadable historical collection, so the old and new can be compared directly, which is often the best way to plan in wild country. France's Institut National de l'Information Géographique et Forestière descends directly from the Cassini survey and publishes the one to twenty five thousand series used by walkers throughout the country. Switzerland's swisstopo produces what most cartographers regard as the finest topographic maps in the world, with two hundred and forty seven sheets at one to twenty five thousand and rock drawing of extraordinary quality. Germany's mapping is run by the individual states around the long established one to twenty five thousand sheet. Canada's National Topographic System covers the country at one to fifty thousand and one to two hundred and fifty thousand, and moved largely to free digital distribution. Japan's Geospatial Information Authority maintains a national base map at one to twenty five thousand. The Survey of India, founded in 1767 and responsible for the Great Trigonometrical Survey that measured the subcontinent, historically restricted access to large scale sheets, a policy substantially relaxed in 2021. Two categories fill the gaps. Military mapping produced under NATO standards, including quarter million operations graphics and fifty thousand line maps, covers much of the world to a uniform specification. More surprisingly, the Soviet Union mapped essentially the entire planet at one to one hundred thousand and one to two hundred thousand during the Cold War, to a consistently high standard, and those sheets became widely available after 1991. For parts of Africa, central Asia and South America they remain the best large scale topographic mapping that has ever existed, decades out of date but geometrically sound. Finally, OpenStreetMap and the renderings derived from it now provide usable topographic coverage in many places that no national agency has ever mapped in detail, at the cost of coverage that varies enormously from one district to the next.

sections.heading: Revision Cycles, Editions and How Maps Go Stale
sections.body: No map is current; every map is a statement about a moment. What separates a usable old map from a dangerous one is knowing which parts of it decay quickly and which do not. Relief is essentially permanent on human timescales. Contours surveyed in 1950 remain correct today except where humans or ice have moved the ground, which happens at quarries, opencast mines, large reservoirs, motorway cuttings and landslips. The dramatic exception of the last half century is glacier ice. Alpine sheets from the 1970s routinely show glacier tongues that now end a kilometre or more further up the valley, and routes drawn across ice may now cross bare rock or a new proglacial lake. Coastlines on soft ground also move, sometimes metres a year, and the low water line on an estuary map is a particularly unreliable feature. Drainage changes slowly, vegetation over decades as plantations are established and felled, and roads and buildings over years. Paths and tracks change fastest of all, and in Britain the legal rights of way shown on a sheet can be altered by administrative order at any time, so a twenty year old Explorer may show a path that has been legally diverted. Revision practice divides into two philosophies. Cyclic revision resurveys each sheet on a schedule, which produces a clear edition history but means that a sheet near the end of its cycle may be very stale indeed; many American quadrangles went thirty or forty years between revisions. Continuous revision, which the Ordnance Survey adopted, updates a central database as changes are detected from aerial imagery, field surveyors and notifications from local authorities, so a printed sheet is a snapshot of a database that was correct when the plate was made. Reading the dates correctly matters more than most people realise, because a sheet may carry four of them and only one is meaningful. Survey date is when somebody measured the ground. Revision date is when detail was last checked and corrected. Photorevision means aerial photographs were interpreted without anybody visiting, which catches new buildings and roads but misses paths under tree cover and gets surfaces wrong. Reprint date means only that more copies were run off, sometimes decades after the last real revision, and a map advertised as a current edition may be a reprint of a 1980s survey. The working rule is straightforward. For terrain, watercourses and general shape, an old sheet is excellent and often better drawn than its replacement. For anything built by people, for tracks, for access and for glaciers, treat anything more than about a decade old as a hypothesis to be checked, ideally against recent satellite imagery before you leave.

sections.heading: Selecting and Preparing Sheets for a Journey
sections.body: Choosing and preparing maps is a short procedure that people routinely skip and then regret. The decisions are all made in advance, at a table, where mistakes cost nothing; every one of them is expensive to discover in weather. The principles behind the sequence are that scale should be the largest that covers the ground in a sensible number of sheets, that sheet edges are the enemy, that any electronic device must be told which model of the Earth the paper uses, and that the magnetic correction printed on a sheet is a historical statement rather than a current one. Work through the following once per trip, and do the whole of it before leaving rather than in the car park.
steps: Define the area you will actually cover including plausible diversions, then pick the largest scale that still fits it into a manageable number of sheets: typically one to twenty five thousand on foot, one to fifty thousand for longer distance travel.

Use the publisher's graphical index to identify the covering sheets, and check whether any part of your route runs within about two kilometres of a sheet edge; if so, obtain the neighbouring sheet as well or buy a custom centred sheet if the agency offers one.
Compare edition dates and buy the most recent, then check the route against recent satellite imagery for new felling, new tracks, washed out bridges and, in mountains, glacier retreat.
Read the marginal geodetic block and note the horizontal datum, the grid and the projection; write them on the map case where you will see them.
Set every electronic device to that same datum and to the grid format you will actually speak on a radio, and confirm by comparing a known point on the map with the device reading before you depart.

Establish the current magnetic correction rather than using the printed one: take the margin value and apply the stated annual change, or better, obtain a current figure from an up to date magnetic model, and write the result on the map face with the date.

Mark the route and build a route card listing each leg with its start and finish grid references, the magnetic bearing already converted, the distance, the height gained and an estimated time using a rate such as five kilometres an hour plus an hour per six hundred metres of ascent.
Identify escape routes off the high ground at intervals along the route and record a grid reference for the top of each, so that a decision to retreat needs no navigation planning at the time.
Weatherproof the sheet by lamination or a sealed case, and if your primary navigation is electronic, carry the paper sheet and a compass as an independent system rather than as a token.
Fold the sheet so the first part of the route is uppermost and refold at planned breaks, and carry a baseplate compass whose romer scales match the scale of the map you are using.

sections.heading: Digital Series, Their Limits and What to Do When Lost
sections.body: Digital mapping has replaced paper for most everyday use, and for good reasons. Position is instant, sheet edges vanish, storage is unlimited, layers can be switched, and elevation models such as the near global thirty metre data set produced by the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission in 2000, or the far finer lidar coverage some countries now publish, allow terrain analysis no printed sheet can offer. Anyone navigating without using these tools is making the job harder than it needs to be. The failure modes, though, are specific and worth rehearsing. The first is loss of context: a phone screen at a zoom level where symbols are legible shows perhaps a square kilometre, so the reader navigates through a straw and loses the sense of the whole day's ground that an unfolded sheet provides. The second is power. Lithium cells lose capacity sharply in cold, and a phone that reads forty per cent charge at room temperature can shut down without warning at minus ten degrees; carrying the device warm against the body rather than in an outer pocket genuinely doubles its useful life. The third is silent positional error. Satellite positioning in the open with a clear sky is typically good to a few metres, but in a steep valley, dense forest or between buildings, signals arrive by reflection and the receiver may report a confident position tens of metres wrong, with no indication that anything is amiss. Height is worse still, commonly two or three times less accurate than horizontal position, which is why a barometric altimeter recalibrated at a known spot height is often the better instrument, remembering that it drifts as the weather changes at roughly eight metres per hectopascal. The fourth is preparation: offline tiles must be deliberately downloaded, at every zoom level you will need, and the moment to discover an empty cache is not on the hill. When map and ground disagree, the discipline is the same whatever technology you are using. Stop walking, because every further step compounds the error. Believe the ground rather than the map; the terrain is real and the map is a document that may be old or misread. Reconstruct the last point at which you were certain of your position, and if you can, return to it. Relocate by terrain association, matching the shape of what you can see to the contours rather than looking for a signpost. Two classical techniques help enormously here. Aiming off means deliberately setting a bearing to one side of a target that lies on a linear feature such as a stream or wall, so that on reaching the feature you know unambiguously which way to turn. A catching feature is something unmissable beyond your objective, a ridge or a road, which tells you when you have gone too far. Both work in zero visibility, with no battery, and they are the reason a compass and a paper sheet remain the system of last resort.

guides.title: Map Scale and What It Really Means
guides.summary: A complete treatment of map scale: how the representative fraction, verbal scale and bar scale work, what large and small scale really mean, how scale governs detail, accuracy and distortion, and how to measure ground distance and travel time from a map in the field.

sections.heading: What Scale Is, and Why Every Map Has One
sections.body:
A map is a shrunken model of a piece of the world, and scale is the number that tells you exactly how much it has been shrunk. Formally, scale is the ratio between a distance measured on the map and the corresponding distance measured on the ground. If one centimetre on the paper stands for fifty thousand centimetres on the earth, the scale is one to fifty thousand, and every other measurement on that sheet obeys the same ratio. Without that number a map is a picture; with it, the map becomes an instrument you can take measurements from.

The idea is old. The Chinese cartographer Pei Xiu, writing around 267 CE, listed a graduated scale as the first of his six principles of mapmaking. What changed in the modern era was standardisation. National agencies settled on fixed series so that any two sheets behave identically: the United States Geological Survey built its topographic coverage at 1:24,000, Britain's Ordnance Survey settled on 1:25,000 and 1:50,000, and most of continental Europe and the military world converged on 1:50,000.

The practical consequence is that scale is not a decoration in the margin. It is the conversion constant for the entire sheet. It determines how far apart two towns are, how long a ridge is, how wide the gap between two crags might be, and whether a stream you can see drawn as a line is a trickle you can step over or a torrent you cannot. It also silently determines what is on the map at all, because a cartographer working at one scale can only draw features above a certain size and must discard or simplify everything smaller.

Two habits separate people who use maps well from people who merely look at them. The first is checking the scale before doing anything else, every single time, because sheets from different series look deceptively similar and a fifty-thousand sheet and a hundred-thousand sheet of the same area can be almost identical in appearance while differing by a factor of two in every distance you take off them. The second is developing a physical intuition: knowing, without arithmetic, that on a 1:50,000 sheet two centimetres is a kilometre, that a typical grid square is a kilometre on a side, and that a fit walker on good ground covers roughly four to five of those squares in an hour. Scale becomes useful only when it stops being a calculation and becomes a feel for distance.

It is worth being clear from the outset about what scale does not tell you. It says nothing about how accurate the original survey was, nothing about how old the information is, and nothing about how much the terrain has changed since the surveyor left. A beautifully drawn 1:25,000 sheet compiled in 1968 will show plantations that were felled decades ago and will miss every road built since. Scale is a statement about resolution, the finest thing the map is capable of expressing, not a guarantee about content or currency. Confusing the two is the root of a great deal of misplaced confidence in the field.

sections.heading: The Three Ways Scale Is Expressed
sections.body:
Scale appears on maps in three interchangeable forms, and a well-made sheet usually carries all three because each survives different kinds of mishandling.

The representative fraction, or RF, is the purest expression. It is written as a ratio with no units at all, such as 1:50,000, sometimes as a true fraction, 1/50,000. Because it carries no units it is self-translating: one of anything on the map equals fifty thousand of the same thing on the ground. One inch equals fifty thousand inches; one millimetre equals fifty thousand millimetres; one thumb-width equals fifty thousand thumb-widths. This unit-independence is what makes the RF the international standard and the form used to name map series. It is also why an RF is meaningless if the map has been resized, since photocopying at ninety percent quietly turns a 1:50,000 map into a 1:55,556 map while the printed fraction still claims otherwise.

The verbal or statement scale expresses the same relationship in convenient everyday units: "one centimetre to one kilometre," "one inch to the mile," "four centimetres to one kilometre." This is the friendliest form for mental arithmetic and the form most walkers actually use. One inch to the mile corresponds to an RF of 1:63,360, because there are 63,360 inches in a statute mile, and that awkward number is precisely why the British one-inch series was eventually replaced by the round metric 1:50,000. Two centimetres to the kilometre is 1:50,000; four centimetres to the kilometre is 1:25,000; one centimetre to the kilometre is 1:100,000.

The bar scale, also called the graphic or linear scale, is a small ruler printed in the margin, subdivided into ground units and usually carrying an extension to the left of zero divided into finer increments. To use it you mark a distance on the edge of a piece of paper, lay it against the bar and read the ground distance directly, with no arithmetic at all. Its great virtue is that it is drawn on the map, so it shrinks and stretches with the map. A bar scale remains truthful after any amount of photocopy reduction, faxing, screenshotting or on-screen zooming, which is exactly when the printed representative fraction becomes a lie.

Converting between the forms is straightforward once you fix your units. To turn an RF into a verbal scale in metric, divide the denominator by 100,000 to get kilometres per map centimetre: 1:25,000 gives 0.25 km per centimetre, or equivalently four centimetres per kilometre. To go the other way, express both sides in the same unit and cancel. The arithmetic is trivial, but doing it once at the start of a trip and writing the answer on the map margin saves fumbling later in wind and rain.

sections.heading: Working the Arithmetic: From Map Millimetres to Ground Kilometres
sections.body:
The conversion is one multiplication, but it is worth doing slowly once so the structure is obvious. Ground distance equals map distance multiplied by the scale denominator. The only trap is units, and the only cure is to keep everything in the same unit until the final step.

Take a 1:50,000 sheet and a measured map distance of 87 millimetres. Multiply: 87 mm times 50,000 gives 4,350,000 millimetres. Divide by 1,000 to reach metres, giving 4,350 metres, and by 1,000 again for kilometres, giving 4.35 km. The shortcut worth memorising is that for any scale, the denominator divided by one million gives kilometres per map millimetre. At 1:50,000 that is 0.05 km per millimetre, so 87 millimetres is 87 times 0.05, or 4.35 km, obtained in one step. At 1:25,000 the factor is 0.025 km per millimetre; at 1:100,000 it is 0.1, which makes that scale the easiest of all for mental work since map millimetres are simply hundred-metre units.

The reverse calculation matters just as often. To find how much map length a known ground distance occupies, divide by the denominator. On a 1:25,000 sheet, 600 metres of ground is 600,000 millimetres divided by 25,000, which is 24 millimetres. This is how you set a bearing leg before you walk it, and how you judge whether a feature will even be distinguishable: if the thing you are looking for spans thirty metres of ground, it occupies 1.2 millimetres on that sheet, about the width of a pencil line.

Imperial work follows the same pattern with less friendly constants. On a 1:24,000 USGS quadrangle, one inch is 24,000 inches, which is 2,000 feet, which is 0.3788 miles. A convenient practical figure is that 2.64 inches is one mile, and that the standard quadrangle, spanning 7.5 minutes of latitude and longitude, is about 6.8 miles tall and between 5.5 and 6.2 miles wide depending on latitude, since lines of longitude converge toward the poles.

A useful discipline is to write the two constants you actually need directly onto the map margin before you set off: kilometres per map millimetre, and map millimetres per hundred metres. On a 1:50,000 sheet those are 0.05 and 2 respectively. On a 1:25,000 sheet they are 0.025 and 4. With those two numbers written down, every field calculation becomes a single multiplication you can do cold, wet and tired, which is the only condition under which the calculation ever actually matters.

Areas behave differently and this catches people out constantly. Area scales as the square of the linear scale. A square centimetre on a 1:50,000 map represents 50,000 times 50,000 square centimetres, which is 2.5 billion square centimetres, or 0.25 square kilometres, that is 25 hectares. Move to 1:25,000 and a square centimetre covers only 6.25 hectares, one quarter as much. So a lake that occupies a satisfying patch of one map covers a quarter of the area on a map of twice the linear scale. Whenever you estimate burned area, snowfield extent, field size or lake surface, remember to square the ratio.

sections.heading: Large Scale Versus Small Scale: The Terminology Everyone Gets Backwards
sections.body:
No piece of map vocabulary causes more confusion than large and small scale, and the confusion is entirely reasonable, because the words point the opposite way from ordinary speech. A large-scale map covers a small area in great detail. A small-scale map covers a large area with little detail. People say "large scale" when they mean "big picture" and are, in cartographic terms, exactly wrong.

The logic becomes clear the moment you treat the representative fraction as an actual fraction. One over twenty-five thousand is a larger number than one over one million, in the same way that one half is larger than one hundredth. So 1:25,000 is a large scale and 1:1,000,000 is a small scale. The rule of thumb is that the smaller the denominator, the larger the scale, and the larger the scale, the more the map zooms in. If the terminology still slips, the reliable mental check is that a large-scale map makes objects appear large.

Rough conventional bands help. Scales from about 1:1,000 to 1:25,000 are large scale: cadastral plans, engineering site drawings, city plans, detailed walking maps. Anything from roughly 1:25,000 to 1:250,000 sits in the medium band that covers most topographic series and road atlases. Below 1:250,000, running out to 1:1,000,000 and beyond into continental and world maps, is small scale. These boundaries are conventions rather than laws, and different national agencies and disciplines draw them in slightly different places; an engineer's idea of large scale starts far larger than a geographer's.

The distinction is not pedantry, because it predicts what a map can and cannot do. Large-scale maps show individual buildings, field boundaries, single trees, footbridges, the exact bend of a stream. They are what you need to find a specific gate in the dark. Small-scale maps show the shape of a mountain range, the pattern of a river system, the relationship between cities. They are what you need to decide which valley to enter in the first place. Neither is better; they answer different questions, and a competent trip carries both, using the small-scale sheet for planning and the large-scale sheet for execution.

There is also a resource dimension. Because area scales as the square of the linear ratio, covering a country at 1:25,000 requires sixteen times as many sheets as covering it at 1:100,000. This is why complete large-scale national coverage is expensive, slowly updated, and in many parts of the world simply does not exist, while small-scale coverage of the entire planet has been available for a century. When you find that the only map of a region is 1:250,000, that is usually a statement about survey economics rather than about the terrain.

sections.heading: The Standard Series and What Each One Actually Gives You
sections.body:
Knowing the numbers is less useful than knowing what each common scale feels like on the ground, so it is worth walking through the working series one at a time.

At 1:10,000 and larger, you are in the realm of plans rather than maps. Individual buildings appear in true outline, fences and walls are distinguishable, and a person can identify which side of a hedge a path runs. Urban emergency services, utility crews, orienteers and archaeologists work here. Orienteering maps, typically 1:10,000 or 1:15,000 with a five metre contour interval, are the most detailed navigational maps most people will ever hold.

At 1:25,000, one kilometre is four centimetres and a standard one-kilometre grid square is a generous four-centimetre box. This is the classic walking scale in Britain and much of Europe. Field boundaries are shown, footpaths are distinguishable from tracks, and small features like sheepfolds and springs appear. The cost is coverage: a day's long walk can run off the edge of the sheet, and the paper is bulky in wind.

At 1:50,000, one kilometre is two centimetres. Field boundaries vanish, minor detail is generalised, but the sheet covers roughly four times the ground of a 1:25,000 sheet of the same paper size. Most military mapping worldwide is 1:50,000, and for open hill country with strong relief it is arguably the better choice, because the terrain shape rather than the fence lines is what you navigate by. A typical sheet covers a region you could genuinely walk across in a few days.

At 1:100,000 to 1:250,000, you have left detailed navigation behind. These are route-planning, cycling, expedition-overview and aviation-adjacent scales. A village becomes a dot, a river becomes a smoothed line, and contour intervals widen to fifty or a hundred metres so only major landforms remain legible. The US 1:250,000 series, each sheet covering one degree of latitude by two of longitude, was for decades the only complete coverage of Alaska.

At 1:500,000 and 1:1,000,000, you are looking at aeronautical charts and continental overviews. The International Map of the World, proposed by Albrecht Penck in 1891 and never completed, was to be a uniform 1:1,000,000 global series.

Sheet size interacts with all of this. Most national series print on paper around 80 by 90 centimetres before folding. At 1:25,000 that covers roughly 20 by 22 kilometres; at 1:50,000, 40 by 45 kilometres; at 1:250,000, 200 by 225 kilometres. So the choice of scale is simultaneously a choice about how many sheets you must carry and how often you will be standing at a sheet edge trying to match two pieces of paper in the wind, which is one of the more miserable experiences in navigation and a good argument for planning routes that sit comfortably inside a single sheet where possible.

The practical lesson is to match scale to the decision you are making. Choosing a valley is a small-scale question. Finding the crossing point of a river in fog is a large-scale question. Trying to answer the second with a map made for the first is the most common preventable navigational error there is.

sections.heading: The Bar Scale: Why the Ruler Printed on the Map Outlives the Number
sections.body:
The bar scale looks like the humblest thing in the margin and is often the most trustworthy element on the whole sheet. It is a short ruler drawn to the map's own scale, divided into ground units, with the zero placed some way in from the left end and the portion to the left of zero, called the extension or the primary scale, subdivided into finer increments. That layout is deliberate. You lay a straight edge with your measured distance against the bar so that the right-hand end falls on a whole unit mark to the right of zero, then read the fractional remainder off the finely divided extension to the left. It gives you a precise reading without any need to interpolate by eye between coarse divisions.

Its structural advantage is that it is part of the drawing. Any process that changes the size of the map changes the bar scale by exactly the same proportion, so the bar remains correct while the representative fraction printed beside it becomes false. This matters far more than it used to. A map photocopied to fit a pocket, a sheet reduced to fit a laminator, a chart photographed on a phone and pinched to fit a screen, a PDF printed with the "fit to page" box ticked: every one of these silently rescales the image. The number in the margin still says 1:50,000. The bar scale still tells the truth.

Using it well takes a small amount of technique. The classic field method is the paper-strip: take any straight-edged scrap, lay it along the route, mark the start, pivot the strip at each bend of the path so the edge follows the line, and tick off each segment cumulatively. When you reach the end you have the whole crooked route captured as a single straight length on the strip, which you then lay against the bar scale and read off. For curved features a length of thread or a shoelace laid along the curve and then straightened against the bar works better than any ruler.

Many maps carry several bars: kilometres, statute miles, nautical miles, and on marine charts, cables and fathoms. Reading the wrong bar is a real and recurring error, particularly the mile-versus-nautical-mile confusion, since a nautical mile of 1,852 metres is fifteen percent longer than a statute mile of 1,609 metres. Aviation and marine charts default to nautical miles; land maps almost never do.

One limitation deserves stating plainly. A bar scale, like the representative fraction, describes the map's nominal scale. On any map covering a large area, the true scale varies from place to place because of projection distortion, and the printed bar is only strictly accurate along particular lines. On a walking sheet covering forty kilometres this error is negligible. On a world map it can be enormous.

sections.heading: Measuring Distance Along a Real Route
sections.body:
Measuring a straight line between two points is easy and almost never what you need. Real routes bend, and the difference between the straight-line distance and the distance you will actually walk is routinely thirty to sixty percent in hill country and can exceed a factor of two on a switchbacked path or an indented coastline.

Several practical methods exist, each with its own accuracy. The paper-strip method described earlier is the most generally useful because it needs nothing but the map and a scrap of paper. A piece of thin string or a bootlace laid carefully along the route, then pulled straight against the bar scale, handles curves better and is what most guidebook writers actually used before software. A map wheel or opisometer, a small toothed wheel on a dial, is run along the route and then run backwards along the bar scale until the dial returns to zero; it is fast but consistently under-reads on tight bends because the wheel cuts corners. Digital mapping software will compute the length instantly and, on modern services, will follow the actual path geometry, which is far more accurate than any hand method.

For a bearing-and-pacing leg, do not measure with a ruler at all if the map carries a grid. Count grid squares. On any metric topographic map with a one-kilometre grid, the diagonal of a square is 1.414 km and the side is exactly one kilometre regardless of the sheet's scale, which is the single most useful fact about grids. You can estimate a leg to within about fifty metres by eye in bad weather with wet gloves.

Two systematic errors deserve naming. The first is the coastline paradox, described by Lewis Fry Richardson in the 1950s and later made famous by Benoit Mandelbrot's 1967 paper asking how long the coast of Britain is. The answer is that it depends entirely on the length of your measuring stick: a shorter stick follows more inlets and yields a longer total, without limit. The same applies to any irregular feature. A stream measured at 1:250,000 will be materially shorter than the same stream measured at 1:25,000, not because either map is wrong but because the finer map preserves wiggles the coarser one smoothed away. Distances quoted for rivers, borders and coastlines are therefore always scale-dependent, and comparing two figures from different sources is meaningless unless both used the same source scale.

The second is simple accumulation. Every pivot of the paper strip introduces a small angular error, and on a route with forty bends those errors compound. As a rule of thumb, add five to ten percent to any hand-measured winding route, and treat any measurement finer than the width of your pencil line as false precision. On a 1:50,000 map a 0.5 mm pencil line is twenty-five metres wide on the ground.

sections.heading: Horizontal Distance, Slope Distance and the Ground You Actually Walk
sections.body:
Every map distance is a horizontal distance. Maps are projections onto a flat reference surface, so the length you measure between two points is the length of their separation as seen from directly above, not the length of the surface you will travel over. On flat ground the difference is nil. On a mountainside it is substantial, and on a scree slope it is the difference between a comfortable day and a benighted one.

The geometry is a right triangle. If the horizontal map distance is H and the height gained is V, the true slope distance D is the square root of H squared plus V squared. Climbing 400 metres over a horizontal kilometre gives a slope distance of the square root of 1,000,000 plus 160,000, which is 1,077 metres, about eight percent longer. That sounds small, and here is the important and counterintuitive point: for ordinary terrain the slope-distance correction is almost negligible. Even a punishing thirty-degree slope adds only fifteen percent to the distance. The correction becomes significant only above about twenty-five degrees, and below about ten degrees it is smaller than your measuring error.

What is not negligible is the time cost of climbing, and this is where the real error lives. The classic correction is Naismith's rule, published by the Scottish mountaineer William Naismith in 1892: allow one hour for every three miles, roughly five kilometres, on the flat, plus an additional hour for every 2,000 feet, roughly 600 metres, of ascent. That works out at about ten extra minutes per hundred metres of climb. Under Naismith, a five-kilometre walk with 600 metres of ascent takes two hours, not one, so ascent doubled the time while adding only a few percent to the distance.

Naismith's rule is optimistic and assumes a fit walker on good ground with a light pack. Several refinements exist. Tranter's corrections scale the Naismith figure by individual fitness and by fatigue over a long day, and can double the estimate for a tired party. Aitken's variant slows the base pace on rough or pathless ground. Langmuir added a descent correction, subtracting ten minutes per 300 metres for gentle descents but adding ten minutes per 300 metres for steep ones, since very steep descent is slower, not faster, than level walking. Modern Tobler hiking-function models express walking speed as a smooth exponential decay with slope, peaking slightly downhill at about minus two-and-a-half degrees rather than on the flat.

In the field, the honest practice is to derive a time from the map, then ask what could make it wrong: deep snow, thick heather, boulder fields, river crossings, heavy packs, darkness, altitude, a party moving at its slowest member's pace. Each of these can add fifty percent. A map distance is a floor on effort, never an estimate of it.

sections.heading: Generalisation: What the Cartographer Deleted on Your Behalf
sections.body:
Scale does not merely shrink the world; it forces the mapmaker to throw things away. This process is called generalisation, and understanding it is the difference between reading a map and trusting it blindly.

The constraint is physical. Printed symbols cannot go below roughly 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres and remain visible, and lines below about 0.15 millimetres disappear or clog. At 1:50,000, a 0.2 millimetre mark represents ten metres on the ground, so nothing smaller than about ten metres can be drawn to true size. At 1:250,000 that same minimum mark represents fifty metres. Everything below the threshold must be dropped, enlarged out of proportion, or merged with a neighbour.

Cartographers work through a recognised set of operations. Selection discards whole categories: at 1:250,000 individual buildings vanish and only settlements remain. Simplification removes vertices from lines, so a meandering river becomes a smoother curve and a jagged coast loses its inlets. Smoothing rounds the remaining angles. Aggregation merges a cluster of small features into one area, so a scatter of ponds becomes a single marsh symbol. Displacement shifts features apart so they do not overlap: where a road, a railway and a river squeeze through the same gorge, all three are drawn wider apart than they really are, sometimes by a hundred metres or more on the ground. Exaggeration keeps a critical but tiny feature visible by drawing it oversize, which is why a road on a 1:250,000 map, if scaled honestly, would be half a kilometre wide.

The navigational consequences are concrete and occasionally serious. A road symbol's width is not the road's width. Two paths shown as separate may be a single braided track on the ground, or the reverse. A stream drawn as one clean line may be a fan of channels. On small-scale maps the displacement of features in congested corridors means the map's internal geometry is locally wrong by more than the scale would suggest. Where the map shows a gap between a cliff edge and a path, that gap may be an artefact of symbol displacement rather than real ground.

There are attempts to formalise the trade-off. Töpfer's radical law, published by Friedrich Töpfer in 1966, estimates how many features should survive a scale reduction: the number retained equals the original number multiplied by the square root of the ratio of the source scale denominator to the target scale denominator. Reducing from 1:25,000 to 1:100,000 gives a factor of the square root of one quarter, that is one half, so roughly half the features should be dropped. It is a guideline, not a law of nature, but it captures the right order of magnitude.

The working attitude is this: a large-scale map is a claim that something exists at that location; a small-scale map is a claim that something exists somewhere near it.

sections.heading: Contours, Vertical Interval and the Scale of Relief
sections.body:
Scale governs the horizontal dimension, but relief has a scale of its own, set by the contour interval, and the two are chosen together.

A contour is a line joining points of equal elevation. The contour interval, or vertical interval, is the height difference between adjacent contours, and it is stated in the map margin. Common values track the scale: five metres or ten metres at 1:25,000, ten or twenty metres at 1:50,000, fifty metres at 1:250,000, and as little as one metre on engineering and orienteering plans. Metre-based series generally use ten metres as the workhorse; foot-based series use twenty, forty or eighty feet. Index contours, drawn thicker and labelled, appear every fifth line to make counting quick.

The interval is chosen so contours stay legible on the steepest ground in the sheet. If the interval is too small on a mountain map, contours merge into a black smear on the crags; too large on gentle country and a whole landscape of subtle valleys and knolls vanishes into blank white paper. Some agencies print supplementary contours at half the standard interval, usually dashed, in areas too flat for the main interval to say anything useful.

Horizontal spacing between contours encodes slope, and this is where map scale and vertical interval interact. Slope angle is the arctangent of the vertical interval divided by the horizontal ground distance between contours. On a 1:50,000 map with a 20-metre interval, contours one millimetre apart mean 20 metres of rise over 50 metres of ground, which is a gradient of 0.4, about 22 degrees, steep enough to be hard work and awkward in snow. Contours half a millimetre apart double that to nearly 39 degrees, which is approaching the limit of what most people will walk without hands. Learning the spacing that corresponds to 30 degrees on your usual sheet, and recognising it instantly, is one of the most valuable skills in mountain navigation, because 30 degrees is roughly the angle at which slab avalanches release and at which a slip becomes an uncontrolled slide.

Beware the profile trap. When you draw or read a cross-section, the vertical axis is almost always exaggerated relative to the horizontal, often by a factor of five or ten, because otherwise the profile of a real mountain range across a hundred kilometres would be an almost flat line. Vertical exaggeration makes gentle hills look like fangs. A slope that appears near-vertical in a printed profile may be a comfortable fifteen degrees. Always check the two axis scales before believing a profile's shape, and compute the exaggeration factor by dividing the horizontal scale denominator by the vertical one.

Contours also fail in specific places: they cannot show overhangs, they are conventionally omitted or dashed under permanent ice where the surface moves, and on very steep rock they are often replaced by cliff hachures that give shape but not measurable height.

sections.heading: Projection, Distortion, and Why Scale Is Not Constant Across a Map
sections.body:
The printed scale of a map is a nominal scale, sometimes called the principal scale, and it is exactly true only along certain lines or at certain points. Everywhere else the true scale differs, sometimes trivially and sometimes enormously. The cause is unavoidable geometry.

The earth's surface is doubly curved and cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing. This is not an engineering limitation but a theorem: Carl Friedrich Gauss proved in his Theorema Egregium of 1827 that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic to a surface and preserved by any bending that does not stretch, so a sphere with positive curvature can never be mapped onto a plane with zero curvature without distortion. Every projection therefore distorts something: area, shape, distance, direction, or some combination.

Cartographers describe the local error with the scale factor, the ratio of true local scale to nominal scale. A scale factor of 1.000 means locally perfect; 1.0004 means distances read four parts in ten thousand too short. The Universal Transverse Mercator system, the grid underlying most military and topographic mapping, divides the world into sixty zones each six degrees of longitude wide and applies a deliberate central scale factor of 0.9996. This slight shrinkage at the zone's central meridian buys accuracy at the zone edges: the scale factor rises through 1.0000 along two lines about 180 km either side of the centre and reaches roughly 1.0010 at the zone boundary. The maximum error is thus about one part in a thousand, one metre per kilometre, which is negligible for walking and significant for surveying.

The Mercator projection, devised by Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for marine navigation, illustrates the extreme case. It preserves angles, which is why a constant compass bearing plots as a straight line, an enormous practical virtue at sea. But its scale factor is the secant of the latitude, so at 60 degrees north it is 2, and at 80 degrees it is about 5.76. Greenland, spanning high latitudes, appears comparable in size to Africa while being about fourteen times smaller. A single bar scale on a Mercator world map is therefore close to meaningless; better sheets print a latitude-varying scale or a set of bars labelled by latitude.

The practical rules follow directly. On a large-scale topographic sheet covering a few tens of kilometres, projection distortion is far below your measuring error and can be ignored entirely. On a regional map spanning several degrees, it becomes visible. On a hemispheric or world map, never measure distance with the bar scale unless the projection is explicitly equidistant along the line you are measuring, and remember that equidistant projections are true only from specific points or along specific lines, never everywhere at once.

Great-circle distance is the honest answer for long routes, and on most projections a great circle is not a straight line on the paper.

sections.heading: The Grid as a Built-In Ruler
sections.body:
Most modern topographic maps carry a rectangular grid of blue or black lines, and that grid is the fastest and most reliable distance tool on the sheet, because unlike the bar scale it is distributed everywhere and needs no measuring instrument.

On metric mapping the grid is almost always one kilometre square, whatever the map's scale. At 1:25,000 the squares are four centimetres across, at 1:50,000 two centimetres, at 1:100,000 one centimetre. Consequently you can read distance directly by counting squares and estimating tenths, and the answer is in kilometres without any conversion. The diagonal of a square is 1.414 km; half a square is 500 metres; a tenth of a square edge is 100 metres. These four numbers cover most field estimation.

The grid is also the basis of position reporting. In the UK Ordnance Survey National Grid and in the military grid reference system, a grid reference is built by reading eastings first, then northings, always right and then up. A four-figure reference identifies a one-kilometre square; six figures identify a hundred-metre box; eight figures identify ten metres; ten figures identify one metre. Interpolating tenths of a square by eye at 1:50,000 means judging two-millimetre steps, which is realistically accurate to about fifty metres in the field, so quoting an eight-figure reference read by eye from a 1:50,000 sheet is false precision. A romer, a small transparent card with graduated corners cut for specific scales, removes the guesswork and is worth carrying; many compasses have romers moulded into the baseplate for the common scales.

There is a subtlety with north. A map has three norths. True north points at the geographic pole. Grid north is the direction of the grid's vertical lines, which parallel the projection's central meridian and therefore diverge from true north by an amount called grid convergence, up to about three degrees at the edge of a UTM zone. Magnetic north is where the compass points, and it differs from true north by the magnetic declination or variation, which varies with location and drifts with time by fractions of a degree a year. The map margin carries a diagram giving all three and the annual rate of change. Confusing grid and magnetic north is a routine cause of navigational error, and at high latitudes, where declination can exceed thirty degrees, it is a serious one.

The grid also lets you check a map's integrity. If you suspect a sheet has been rescaled by copying, measure a grid square. If it is not the expected two or four centimetres, the printed representative fraction is wrong and only the bar scale, which shrank with everything else, can be trusted. This thirty-second check has saved a great many badly-planned days.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Scale for the Task
sections.body:
Choosing a scale is a matter of matching the map's resolving power to the size of the decision you must make, and to the pace at which you are travelling.

Speed is the first filter. A walker covers four to five kilometres an hour, which at 1:25,000 is sixteen to twenty centimetres of map. That is a comfortable rate of page consumption, and it gives time to read the fine detail the scale offers. A cyclist at twenty kilometres an hour crosses eighty centimetres of a 1:25,000 sheet in an hour and will be refolding the map constantly; 1:100,000 or 1:150,000 suits better. A driver at ninety kilometres an hour wants 1:250,000 or smaller. A light aircraft at 200 km/h uses 1:500,000 sectionals. The rule is to choose a scale where the distance covered in roughly an hour is a comfortable span of map, on the order of ten to twenty centimetres.

The second filter is what you need to identify. If the navigation problem is "which of these three side valleys," a 1:50,000 or even 1:100,000 map answers it. If the problem is "the gate through the wall is somewhere along this kilometre of boundary," you need 1:25,000 or better. In featureless terrain such as moorland plateau, forest, or desert, detail matters more than usual because there is so little to fix on, so go larger scale than the distance alone suggests. In dramatic terrain with unmistakable landmarks, a smaller scale is often perfectly adequate and lighter to carry.

The third filter is weather and light. Fine detail is unreadable in driving rain, at night under a head torch, or in whiteout. Under those conditions navigation collapses back onto bearings, pacing and gross relief, all of which work fine at 1:50,000. Carrying a huge, detailed sheet that you cannot actually read in the conditions you expect is a common mistake.

Practical strategy for a serious trip is layered. Carry one small-scale overview covering the entire region for escape routes, road access and the shape of the country, and one large-scale sheet for the ground you will actually cross, ideally cropped and laminated or in a case. Print custom extracts if the software allows it, and always print the bar scale and the grid with them.

Digital adds a trap here. On-screen maps let you zoom continuously, but the underlying data was compiled at a fixed scale and does not gain detail when magnified. Zooming a 1:250,000 dataset to look like 1:25,000 produces a large, smooth, confident picture containing 1:250,000 information. This is scale inflation, and it is the digital equivalent of enlarging a low-resolution photograph. Always know the source scale of the data, not just the display scale.

sections.heading: Scale on Screens: Zoom Levels, Pixels and Ground Sample Distance
sections.body:
Digital mapping changed the relationship between scale and the map in ways that are easy to miss, and the changes matter for anyone whose primary map is a phone.

A printed map has one fixed scale. A screen map has at least three quantities that people all call scale. The first is the display scale, the ratio between screen distance and ground distance right now, which changes every time you pinch. The second is the source or compilation scale of the data, fixed when the data was surveyed and generalised. The third, for imagery and elevation data, is the ground sample distance, the real-world size of one pixel: 10 metres for Sentinel-2 optical bands, about 30 metres for classic Landsat, sub-metre for commercial satellites, and typically 30 metres for the global SRTM elevation model derived from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission.

Web maps organise themselves into discrete zoom levels rather than continuous scale. The near-universal scheme, inherited from Google Maps and adopted by the OpenStreetMap ecosystem, starts at zoom level 0 with the whole world in a single 256-pixel tile and doubles the linear resolution at each level. At the equator, level 0 gives about 156 kilometres per pixel; each level halves it, so level 10 is about 152 metres per pixel, level 15 about 4.8 metres, and level 19 about 0.3 metres. Because the underlying projection is Web Mercator, these figures must be multiplied by the cosine of the latitude, so at 60 degrees north every pixel covers half the ground it does at the equator, and the map is locally twice as large in scale as the nominal zoom implies.

Two consequences follow. First, a device's reported scale bar is honest about the display but says nothing about data quality; a beautifully smooth rendering at zoom 17 may be drawing on data compiled at 1:250,000, and the smoothness is interpolation, not information. Second, a screen shows very little map. A phone screen is roughly 7 by 15 centimetres. Displayed at true 1:25,000, that is 1.75 by 3.75 kilometres of ground, less than one percent of what a paper sheet shows at once. This is why people using phones frequently have excellent local detail and no idea of the wider situation, an error paper users rarely make. The discipline is to deliberately zoom out at every stop.

Finally, GPS position accuracy interacts with scale. A consumer receiver under open sky achieves roughly three to five metres horizontally, degrading to tens of metres in canyons, dense forest or beside cliffs through multipath. At 1:25,000 a five-metre error is 0.2 millimetres, invisible. At 1:250,000 it is 0.02 millimetres, absurdly small. The dot on the screen is therefore almost always more precise than the map it sits on, which creates a dangerous false confidence: the position is right, but the depicted feature beside it may be generalised, displaced or fifty years out of date.

sections.heading: Accuracy Standards, Datums and How Much to Trust a Position
sections.body:
Scale sets the limit of what a map can show, but published accuracy standards set what it promises, and the two are different things worth separating.

The long-standing United States National Map Accuracy Standards, issued in 1947, specify that for maps at scales larger than 1:20,000, no more than ten percent of well-defined test points may be in error by more than one-thirtieth of an inch measured on the map; for scales of 1:20,000 and smaller the tolerance is one-fiftieth of an inch. On a 1:24,000 quadrangle, one-fiftieth of an inch is 0.508 millimetres, which at that scale is about 12.2 metres on the ground. So a well-surveyed USGS quad promises that ninety percent of identifiable points sit within roughly twelve metres of their true position. Vertical accuracy is set at half the contour interval for ninety percent of tested elevations.

Modern standards, such as the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing positional accuracy standards for digital geospatial data, express accuracy in ground units directly rather than as a fraction of map scale, which is more honest for data that will be displayed at any zoom. The practical takeaway is the same: expect a well-defined point to be good to roughly half a millimetre of map, which is twelve metres at 1:24,000, twenty-five metres at 1:50,000 and 125 metres at 1:250,000.

Datum is the other half of the problem and causes larger errors than scale ever does. A datum is the reference model of the earth's shape that coordinates are expressed against. WGS 84, used by GPS, differs from older regional datums by hundreds of metres in some parts of the world: NAD 27 positions in the continental United States differ from WGS 84 by up to about 100 metres, and some older Pacific and African datums differ by several hundred. Entering a WGS 84 coordinate into a map drawn on a different datum, or the reverse, produces a consistent offset that no amount of careful measurement will reveal. The datum is stated in the map margin, and checking it before transferring any coordinate between systems is not optional.

Currency is the third factor and often the worst. A map's scale says nothing about its age. Tracks are built and abandoned, forests are felled and planted, rivers migrate, glaciers retreat, coastlines erode, and buildings appear. Many national series have revision cycles measured in decades, and in some regions the newest available large-scale map is from the 1960s. The margin carries a survey date and a revision date; read both.

The honest summary is that a map position carries three independent uncertainties: what the scale can resolve, what the survey achieved, and how much the world has changed since. Field navigation should always assume the map is approximately right and the ground is definitively right.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: How Scale Errors Actually Hurt People
sections.body:
Scale mistakes rarely announce themselves. They produce plans that look reasonable and then quietly fail, usually late in the day, and the recurring patterns are worth naming so they can be recognised in advance.

The commonest is underestimating a route by measuring straight lines. A ridge walk that measures twelve kilometres point to point may be eighteen kilometres along the actual crest, and with 1,200 metres of ascent, Naismith gives six hours before any allowance for rough ground, navigation stops, or a slow companion. Parties routinely set out on what they believe is a four-hour day and finish in the dark.

The second is misreading the scale of an unfamiliar sheet. This is especially dangerous when moving between countries or between metric and imperial series, because a 1:50,000 and a 1:63,360 sheet look almost identical and differ by 27 percent in every distance. The fix is mechanical: before doing anything else, find the scale, find the grid square size, and find the contour interval, and say all three out loud.

The third is trusting a photocopy or a screenshot. Any reproduction may have been rescaled. If the grid squares do not measure what they should for the stated scale, only the bar scale is valid.

The fourth is scale inflation on digital maps, where zooming coarse data produces an authoritative-looking picture with no additional information in it. The corollary is that a path shown as a clean line on a zoomed-in low-resolution dataset may not exist on the ground at all.

The fifth is confusing map distance with travel distance in genuinely hard terrain. Deep snow, tussock, bamboo, mangrove, boulder fields, thick windthrow and unbridged rivers can reduce progress to under one kilometre per hour. Polar and jungle travellers plan in hours and fuel, not kilometres, precisely because map distance becomes almost uninformative.

The sixth is area estimation without squaring the ratio, which produces errors of a factor of four or sixteen in estimates of burn scars, floodplains, snowfields and crop areas.

The seventh is symbol width taken literally: a river drawn 0.4 millimetres wide on a 1:250,000 map would be a hundred metres across if scaled honestly, and the actual channel may be two metres or two hundred.

When things go wrong, the recovery discipline is the same in every case. Stop and re-derive your position from ground features rather than from your estimate of how far you have come, because a distance error compounds while a terrain fix does not. Re-measure the remaining leg using grid squares rather than memory. Recalculate time with a pessimistic pace, not the one you hoped for. And make the turnaround decision on the clock, not on the map, because the map cannot see the light going.

sections.heading: Building a Working Feel for Scale in the Field
sections.body:
Everything above becomes useful only when it stops being arithmetic and becomes reflex. The good news is that the reflex can be trained deliberately in a few outings, and the training is worth more than any amount of reading.

Start by fixing the constants of the map you use most. For a 1:50,000 sheet: one grid square is one kilometre, two centimetres; a fingernail width is roughly a kilometre; the width of a standard compass baseplate, about 5.5 centimetres, is about 2.75 kilometres; a 20-metre contour interval means contours one millimetre apart is roughly 22 degrees. For a 1:25,000 sheet, halve all the distance figures and double the map lengths. Say these numbers to yourself until they are automatic. In wind and rain you will not do multiplication.

Then calibrate yourself. Pacing is the classic method: on a measured hundred metres of flat ground, count double-paces, meaning every time the same foot lands. Most adults fall between 60 and 70 double-paces per hundred metres. Repeat it uphill, downhill, and on rough ground, because the count changes by ten to twenty percent, and record the numbers on the map case. Combine this with timing: at four kilometres an hour, a hundred metres takes ninety seconds, and knowing your own figure lets you convert a measured map leg into an expected arrival time and then treat overrunning that time as evidence you have made an error, which is the single most useful early-warning signal in navigation.

Practise estimating before measuring. Look at a leg, guess the distance, then check it with grid squares. The gap between guess and truth closes quickly, usually within a dozen repetitions, and once it does you can plan a day's route in thirty seconds rather than five minutes.

Practise the reverse too: on the ground, estimate how far away a visible feature is, then locate it on the map and check. This trains the far more difficult skill of judging real distance visually, which is systematically distorted by terrain. People overestimate distance across broken ground and badly underestimate it across water, snow and desert, sometimes by a factor of two or three, because there are no intermediate objects to give the eye a scale reference.

Finally, build the habit of stating the plan in units you can verify. Not "we go over the col and down to the lake," but "1.8 kilometres on a bearing of 240 grid, about 25 minutes, 120 metres of ascent, and if we have not reached the col in 35 minutes we stop and re-fix." That sentence is entirely built from map scale, and it converts a hopeful intention into a testable prediction. A navigator who makes testable predictions catches errors within minutes. One who does not may not catch them until nightfall.

guides.safetyNote: Distance measured on a map is horizontal distance on an idealised surface. Real travel time depends on slope, vegetation, snow, water crossings and your own condition, and can exceed the map estimate by a factor of three or more. Never commit to a route, a fuel load or a daylight window on map distance alone.

sections.heading: Use the Compass
sections.body:
A magnetic compass does not point at the North Pole. A magnetized needle pivoting on a jewelled bearing aligns with the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, which is generated by convection in the planet's liquid iron outer core, not by geography. The north magnetic pole is a moving target, drifting from about 10 km per year through the twentieth century to 50-60 km per year now as it crosses the Arctic Ocean toward Siberia. The angular gap between where your needle settles and the true geographic pole is called magnetic declination, or variation at sea. Along an agonic line, where the two coincide, declination is zero. In Alaska, the Yukon and the South Island of New Zealand it exceeds 20 degrees, which over a 5 km leg puts you 1.8 km off target. The app's Compass evaluates the World Magnetic Model, a spherical-harmonic description of the global field re-fitted every five years, to convert the phone's raw magnetometer reading into a true-north bearing on the spot. That model lives in the app, which is why the reading survives with no signal.

The field also tips into the ground. Magnetic inclination, or dip, is close to zero at the magnetic equator and approaches 90 degrees near the poles, so a needle completely free to move would stand almost vertical in northern Canada. Hand compasses solve this by counterweighting the needle for one of several global zones, or with a globally balanced needle; a compass bought in Europe can drag or stick in Australia. A phone measures all three field axes and is immune to dip, but it is not immune to drift. The magnetometer needs its offsets re-fitted regularly, which is what the figure-eight waving gesture does; skip it and errors of 10 to 30 degrees are ordinary rather than exceptional.

The other error is deviation: iron and current near the instrument. A belt buckle, a knife, trekking-pole tips, a rucksack frame, rebar in concrete, a chain-link fence, a parked car, high-tension lines and the magnets in the phone's own speaker and case flap all pull the reading. Useful separations are about 1 m from small steel objects, 10 m from a vehicle, and 50 m or more from power lines. Whole hillsides of basalt or magnetite-bearing ore can deflect a needle by tens of degrees, which is why some geological maps carry explicit local-anomaly warnings.

The technique matters more than the instrument. Hold the compass level, take the bearing, then immediately transfer it to something you can see on that line and walk to that object without looking at the needle again. People cannot walk a straight line unaided: blindfolded walkers on open ground spiral into circles roughly 20 m across within a few minutes. Relaying landmark to landmark, and checking a back bearing by adding or subtracting 180 degrees at each one, is what turns a number on a dial into a straight track across the ground. The honest caveat is power: a phone compass dies with the battery, and a baseplate compass costing the price of a sandwich reads to about 2 degrees indefinitely.

sections.heading: Sun
sections.body:
The sun rises somewhere in the eastern half of the sky and sets somewhere in the western half, every day, everywhere on Earth, because the planet turns eastward on its axis. That much is unconditional and it is the single most robust directional fact available to anyone outdoors. What is not unconditional, and what quietly ruins amateur sun navigation, is the popular shorthand that the sun rises due east and sets due west. It does that on exactly two days a year, the March and September equinoxes, and only then.

The rest of the year the sunrise point swings north and south along the horizon with the seasons, because the Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees to its orbit. The size of that swing depends on your latitude, and the relationship is worth carrying in your head: the sine of the rising amplitude, measured away from due east, equals the sine of the sun's declination divided by the cosine of your latitude. At the equator the swing is a modest 23 degrees either side. At 40 degrees north, London-to-Madrid latitudes in Europe or roughly Philadelphia in North America, midsummer sunrise lands near 55-60 degrees on the compass and midwinter sunrise near 120 degrees, a total spread of about 60 degrees. At 60 degrees north the same arithmetic blows out past 100 degrees of spread, and above the Arctic Circle the sun stops rising and setting at all for part of the year. Treating a June sunrise as due east at high latitude is not a small error; it is a 30-degree error that compounds with every kilometre walked.

The reliable moment is local solar noon, when the sun crosses your meridian at its highest point of the day and shadows are at their shortest. At that instant the sun lies exactly due south for any observer north of the Tropic of Cancer, and exactly due north for any observer south of the Tropic of Capricorn. Between the tropics it can be on either side, or directly overhead, so the rule must be applied with knowledge of the date and your latitude rather than by reflex.

Local solar noon is almost never twelve o'clock on a phone. Three separate offsets stack. Daylight saving adds a full hour in summer for most of Europe, North America and Australasia. Longitude within a time zone adds four minutes per degree away from the zone's central meridian, which in a wide zone such as China's single national time or Spain's mismatched zone can reach 40 to 90 minutes. The equation of time, produced by the Earth's elliptical orbit and axial tilt, adds a further wobble of up to about plus-or-minus 16 minutes that peaks in early November and mid-February. Rather than compute all three under pressure, find noon empirically: plant a stick, mark the shadow every few minutes through the middle of the day, and take the shortest shadow you observe. That shadow is your meridian line, accurate to a degree or two, and it needs no clock at all.

sections.heading: Stars (Northern Hemisphere)
sections.body:
Polaris is useful for one reason only, and it is a lucky accident of the current era: it happens to sit within about 0.7 degrees of the north celestial pole, the point about which the entire northern sky appears to rotate. Everything else wheels; Polaris barely moves, tracing a small circle a little over a degree across in the course of a night. Face it and you are facing true north, not magnetic north, with no declination correction and no instrument. This will not last. Precession swings the Earth's axis around a 26,000-year circle, and Polaris only became a usefully close pole star within the last several centuries; it reaches its minimum separation around the year 2100 and then slowly drifts away again. Thuban in Draco held the role when the Egyptian pyramids were built, and Vega will hold it in about 12,000 years.

Finding it is a two-step relay rather than a search, because Polaris is not bright. At magnitude 1.98 it ranks around the fiftieth brightest star in the sky, which is the single most common failure in practice: people scan for a brilliant beacon, pick something far too bright such as Vega, Capella or the planet Jupiter, and walk off on a badly wrong heading. Instead find the Big Dipper, known in Britain as the Plough, a distinctive seven-star pattern within Ursa Major that most people can already recognize. Take the two stars forming the outer wall of its bowl, Dubhe and Merak, which are traditionally called the Pointers. Draw a line from Merak through Dubhe and extend it away from the bowl by about five times the gap between them, roughly 28 to 30 degrees, which is about three fist-widths held at arm's length. The moderately bright star sitting alone at the end of that line, with nothing comparable near it, is Polaris. It is also the last star in the handle of the Little Dipper, Ursa Minor.

The Big Dipper is circumpolar and never sets above about 41 degrees north, but it swings low and can be hidden by trees, hills or haze in the early evening at some times of year. The backup is Cassiopeia, the flattened W or M of five stars on the opposite side of the pole. Polaris lies roughly midway between the Dipper's Pointers and the deeper of Cassiopeia's two V-shaped notches, so whichever of the two patterns is high, the other is low, and one of them is nearly always usable.

Two practical limits. The first is a bonus: the altitude of Polaris above the true horizon equals your latitude to within a degree, so a fist-and-finger estimate of its height gives you a position line as well as a direction, which is how ocean navigators fixed latitude for centuries. The second is a hard boundary: below about 10 degrees north Polaris sits so close to the horizon that haze, hills and refraction make it unreliable, and south of the equator it is gone entirely. (Diagram: AstroOgier, CC0 / public domain.)

sections.heading: Stars (Southern Hemisphere)
sections.body:
The southern sky has no useful pole star. The nearest bright candidate to the south celestial pole is Sigma Octantis, and at magnitude 5.4 it sits at the edge of naked-eye visibility from a dark site and is invisible under streetlights, moonlight or haze. Southern navigation therefore works by geometry: you locate an empty point in the sky by projecting lines from patterns you can see, then drop that point to the horizon to get south.

The primary tool is Crux, the Southern Cross, the smallest constellation in the sky but one of the most distinctive: four bright stars in a kite shape, with a fifth fainter one inside it. Its long axis runs from Gacrux, the orange-tinted star at the top of the kite, through Acrux, the brilliant blue-white star at the foot. Extend that axis beyond Acrux by about four and a half times the length of the cross itself and you arrive at the south celestial pole, a conspicuously blank patch of sky. Drop a vertical line from there straight down to the horizon and where it lands is true south.

The classic and genuinely dangerous mistake is the False Cross, a wider, dimmer, more symmetrical kite formed by stars in Vela and Carina, which lies close by and fools people every season. Three tests separate them. The real Crux is noticeably smaller and more compact; its stars are brighter and unequal, with Gacrux visibly orange against three blue-white companions; and it has the two Pointers, Alpha and Beta Centauri, sitting bright and close alongside it, which the False Cross does not. Alpha Centauri at magnitude minus 0.27 is the third brightest star in the entire sky, so the Pointers are hard to miss and hard to mistake.

The Pointers also provide an independent second method that is more accurate than the Crux extension alone, because it does not depend on estimating a length. Draw the line joining Alpha and Beta Centauri, then construct its perpendicular bisector, a line at right angles through its midpoint. Where that bisector crosses the extended long axis of Crux is the south celestial pole, and the two lines cross at a good angle, so the intersection is well defined rather than a vague guess. This crossing method typically gets you within about 3 to 5 degrees, against 5 to 10 for the axis extension by eye.

There is a third check for very dark skies. The two Magellanic Clouds, faint detached smudges that look like torn-off pieces of the Milky Way, sit on the far side of the pole from Crux, which lies roughly at the apex of a rough equilateral triangle formed with them. Coarse, but a useful sanity check when Crux is low. As in the north, the altitude of the pole above the horizon equals your latitude, so once you have located that blank point you have your latitude for free. And unlike Polaris, Crux is not circumpolar from the low southern latitudes: from about 20 degrees south and northward it sets for part of the night, so learn the Pointers as well, not just the Cross.

sections.heading: Find north by shadow-stick
sections.body:
The shadow-stick works in both hemispheres, at any latitude, on any sunny day, without a clock, a compass, a map or any knowledge of the date, and it is the single most useful improvised direction method there is. The mechanism is straightforward: the sun tracks westward across the sky, so a shadow cast by a fixed vertical object sweeps eastward across the ground at the same rate. Over a short interval the tip of that shadow traces a path that is very nearly a straight line, and that line runs west to east. Crucially the first mark is always the western one, because the shadow moves east as time passes, and this holds in both hemispheres and on the equator alike.

In practice: find flat, open ground clear of slopes and undergrowth, since a shadow falling across a bank or bush distorts where the tip lands. Push a straight stick roughly a metre long into the ground as close to vertical as you can judge, and mark the very tip of the shadow with a pebble or a twig pressed into the soil. That mark is west. Wait, then mark the new tip. Join the two marks and you have a west-east line; stand with the first mark to your left and the second to your right and you are facing north. Set a line at right angles to it and you have north-south.

The wait time is a trade-off, and this is where accuracy is won or lost. Fifteen minutes gives a short baseline; if you misplace either mark by a couple of centimetres, that error is a large fraction of the total shadow travel and the resulting bearing can be off by 10 to 15 degrees. Waiting 30 to 60 minutes lengthens the baseline and shrinks the effect of a sloppy mark, but introduces the opposite error: the shadow tip does not really travel in a straight line, it traces a hyperbola, and the longer you wait the more the curvature bites. The curvature is worst near the solstices and at high latitudes, and it very nearly vanishes near the equinoxes. A reasonable compromise for a rough bearing is 20 to 30 minutes.

For a genuinely accurate result, use the equal-shadow method instead, which cancels the curvature entirely by exploiting the symmetry of the sun's daily arc about local noon. In mid-morning, mark the shadow tip and measure the shadow's length with a piece of cord. Tie the cord to the stick's base and scribe an arc of that exact radius on the ground. In the afternoon, watch until the lengthening shadow tip touches that arc again and mark it. The straight line joining the two marks is a true east-west line good to a degree or two, and the bisector from the stick's base to that line's midpoint points true north-south, because the sun was at the same altitude on either side of noon. It costs a few hours of waiting, which is exactly what you often have while sheltering out the middle of a hot day.

sections.heading: Analog-watch method
sections.body:
The watch method exists because of a simple mismatch in rates. The hour hand of a twelve-hour analog watch goes right around the dial twice a day, which is 720 degrees in 24 hours, or 30 degrees per hour. The sun goes around once, 360 degrees in 24 hours, or 15 degrees per hour. The hour hand therefore moves at exactly twice the sun's angular rate, and halving an angle involving the hour hand brings the two back into step. That is the whole of the trick, and understanding it means you can reconstruct the rule rather than trying to recall which way round it goes under stress.

In the Northern Hemisphere, hold the watch flat and horizontal, face up, and turn your whole body until the hour hand points directly at the sun. The line bisecting the angle between the hour hand and the 12 mark on the dial then points south, and the opposite direction is north. Take the bisector of the smaller of the two angles: before 6 in the morning and after 6 in the evening it is easy to bisect the wrong side and end up 180 degrees out, which is the most common and most consequential failure. In the Southern Hemisphere the rule inverts: point the 12 mark at the sun instead, and the bisector between the 12 and the hour hand points north. A worked example makes it concrete. At 4 in the afternoon, true solar time, in the Northern Hemisphere, the hour hand is on the 4. Point it at the sun. Halfway between the 4 and the 12 on the shorter side is the 2 mark, so the direction the 2 points is south.

The method demands true local solar time, not what the phone says. Undo daylight saving by subtracting the full hour in summer. Correct for longitude within your time zone at four minutes per degree of longitude from the zone's central meridian, which can be worth 30 to 60 minutes or more in wide or politically stretched zones such as western Spain, western China or Alaska. The equation of time adds up to a further 16 minutes either way. Get these wrong by an hour, as unconverted daylight saving does, and the bisector rotates by 7.5 degrees.

Now the honest caveat that most survival books omit. The watch method assumes the sun moves along an arc perpendicular to the horizon at a steady 15 degrees per hour of azimuth, and that assumption is only reasonable at middle and high latitudes, and best in winter.
